triggers: a kernel on NVIDIA B200 (GB200 / SM100) risks the '4. `tl.static_range` unroll blows up past a small tile-bytes threshold' trap

payload.goal: Avoid a known trap on NVIDIA B200 (GB200 / SM100): 4. `tl.static_range` unroll blows up past a small tile-bytes threshold

problem.statement: sm_100 Triton sparse-decode / split-K pitfalls -- 4. `tl.static_range` unroll blows up past a small tile-bytes threshold

payload.attempted: `tl.static_range(N)` unrolls the loop for ILP — sounds strictly better than dynamic `range()`.
payload.lesson: `static_range(N)` is a win when **`N × tile_bytes ≲ 8 KB`** per iter; it regresses at ≥16 iters or ≥32-KB tiles. Don't switch static↔dynamic on iteration count alone — decide on per-iter tile footprint.

established_fact.mechanism: Unrolling helps when the per-iter body is small and serial (interleaves iter `i` compute with iter `i+1` loads); it hurts when each iter loads multi-KB tiles (the inlined N copies exhaust registers/icache).

payload.observed: `static_range(16)` loading a 32-KB tile/iter ran **5× slower** than dynamic `range()` (register/icache blowup). But at the other extreme, switching a *small-body* combine loop from `static_range(16)` to `range(16)` **regressed +5-7%** — the unroll was buying real cross-iter ILP that `num_stages` (only ~1-2 iters ahead) couldn't.
payload.root_cause: Unrolling helps when the per-iter body is small and serial (interleaves iter `i` compute with iter `i+1` loads); it hurts when each iter loads multi-KB tiles (the inlined N copies exhaust registers/icache).
